messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 38-year-old Lebanese-American hairdresser who works at a mid-range salon in a mid-sized city, a man who built his professional identity around physical touch, sensory precision, and the quiet intimacy of caring for others. Eighteen months ago, that identity was violently interrupted when he was hospitalised for what initially presented as a severe respiratory infection and was rapidly diagnosed as a life-threatening case of bacterial sepsis. Over eleven days in the ICU, Tariq underwent repeated invasive procedures — central line insertions, blood draws every few hours, a brief period on supplemental oxygen delivered through a tight-fitting mask. He remembers the smell of the ICU with a particular clarity that still disturbs him: a combination of antiseptic, plastic tubing, and something underneath it that he can only describe as "the smell of being very close to not existing." He recalls a moment, around the fourth day, when the pain in his chest and arms was so severe that he was certain he was dying, and that certainty — that his own body had turned against him without warning — became the lens through which he has interpreted nearly everything since.

In the months following his discharge, Tariq found that certain experiences would pull him back toward the hospital with a force that felt physical. Waking from a nightmare left him in a state where his body could not distinguish the present bedroom from the ICU — heart pounding, muscles locked, chest tight — and those mornings became among the most disorienting of his week. Related photographs were another source of unexpected intrusion: a friend once sent him a photo from a hospital fundraiser, and Tariq found himself unable to look away and unable to look at it, his hands trembling, his body flooding with the same physical reactions he had experienced during the worst of his illness. These triggers did not merely recall the event — they seemed to reconstitute it. When something reminded him of those eleven days, he could sometimes smell the antiseptic again, and on worse occasions he felt a dull, spreading ache in his chest and arms in the same places the pain had lived during his hospitalisation, as though the memory were stored in tissue rather than thought. At other times the emotional weight arrived without any accompanying image — a sudden wave of fear or shame with no clear object, which he found even more difficult to explain or manage.

What Tariq found most frightening, however, was not the intrusions themselves but what he had come to believe they meant. He was increasingly certain that his body was no longer trustworthy — that it had failed him once without warning and could do so again at any moment — and this conviction kept him in a state of constant physiological vigilance, muscles perpetually braced, attention perpetually scanning. He had come to believe that reacting this way, months after leaving the hospital, meant something was fundamentally wrong with his mind, that he was, as he put it during intake, "losing the thread of what is real." These appraisals were not inert; believing his body was unreliable and his mind potentially fractured made the intrusive memories feel more threatening when they arrived, amplifying their emotional intensity and making it harder to let them pass. Worse, the appraisals themselves seemed to function as triggers — the moment Tariq noticed his body tensing or his thoughts becoming fragmented, he would begin scanning for evidence of illness or breakdown, and that scanning would pull forward the sensory and emotional residue of the hospitalisation, feeding the very intrusions he was trying to prevent.

The most concrete consequence of this cycle has emerged in his work. Tariq now finds it difficult to perform medical-adjacent tasks — even the routine act of a client mentioning a recent surgery or illness can activate the full cascade. He has begun declining certain clients and has called in sick on days when he knows a client with a chronic condition is scheduled. His income has dropped noticeably, and his colleagues have begun to notice his absences. He remains single, and the social withdrawal that has accompanied his avoidance has deepened his isolation.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a routine dental appointment last month — a medical examination that triggered a panic response so severe he had to leave before it was completed. He arrived at the intake session exhausted and ashamed, hoping above all to be told that he was not going crazy, and afraid, more than anything, that he already was.
